As a reminder, the current quarter includes the full 13-week of Foot Locker results compared to approximately 8 weeks in the prior year period following the acquisition close on September 8, 2025. Consolidated net sales increased 23.2% to $5.13 billion. Within this, the sales of the Foot Locker business increased $866 million due primarily to the additional 5 weeks of Foot Locker ownership. Comp sales for the DICK'S business increased 2.6%, driven by a 3.7% increase in average ticket, partially offset by a 1.1% decline in transactions.

Industry observers note that we delivered a very strong back-to-school season and saw broad-based growth across footwear, team sports, license and trading cards. Warmer weather in October pressured our cold weather categories and contributed to lower transactions, partially offsetting the strength we saw earlier in the quarter. Importantly, the 2.6% comp was on top of a strong 5.7% comp increase from last year. Pro forma comps for the Foot Locker business increased 0.5% for the quarter, driven by a 1.3% increase in North America. Notably, the U.S. Foot Locker banner delivered comp growth of 4.1%. From a margin perspective, consolidated non-GAAP gross profit was $1.66 billion or 32.4% of net sales, down 73 basis points from last year.

The year-over-year decline was primarily driven by the mix impact from the Foot Locker business from the additional ownership period. For the DICK'S business, gross margin declined 26 basis points from last year. This decline was driven by higher occupancy and supply chain-related costs, including higher fuel costs as well as product mix and pricing investment in athletic footwear. These pressures were partially offset by strong growth from DICK'S Media Network and GameChanger. Turning to expenses. On a non-GAAP basis, consolidated SG&A expenses increased 25.1% or $278.4 million to $1.39 billion and deleveraged 42 basis points compared to last year's non-GAAP results. For the DICK'S business, SG&A expenses deleveraged 10 basis points.

According to recent reports, consolidated non-GAAP operating income was $249.7 million or 4.86% of net sales compared to $242.2 million or 5.81% of net sales last year. This includes operating income of $290.6 million or 8.71% of net sales for the DICK'S business and operating loss of $40.9 million for the Foot Locker business. Moving down the P&L. Consolidated non-GAAP income tax expense was $67.2 million or a rate of 28.6%. Our effective tax rate for the quarter was shaped by the mix of our earnings in foreign jurisdictions. In total, we delivered consolidated non-GAAP earnings per diluted share of $1.94 for the quarter. This compares to non-GAAP earnings per diluted share of $2.07 last year.

Sources indicate that on a GAAP basis, our earnings per diluted share were $1.87. For additional details, you can refer to the non-GAAP reconciliation tables of our press release that we issued this morning. Now looking to our balance sheet. We ended the quarter with approximately $464 million of cash and cash equivalents and no borrowings on our $2 billion unsecured credit facility. Inventory was $6.1 billion at the end of the quarter, an increase of 9% versus last year. Within this, inventory for the DICK'S business increased 5.7%, while inventory for Foot Locker business increased 15.8%.

Sources indicate that at Foot Locker, the inventory growth reflects a combination of planned investments in new and differentiated brands and styles as well as higher-than-desired inventory in certain legacy franchises following the shift in consumer demand we discussed last quarter. We are taking appropriate action to address this through markdowns, returns and cancellation of the product on order. Turning to capital allocation for the quarter. We remain committed to maintaining a strong balance sheet, while investing in the business and returning capital to shareholders. During the quarter, net capital expenditures were $335 million, and we returned $110 million to shareholders through dividends. As Ed discussed, we took advantage of the dislocation in our stock price during the quarter.

We completed a $1 billion senior notes offering and repurchased 6.7 million shares of our stock for $903 million at an average price of $134.21. Year-to-date, we have repurchased 7.4 million shares for $1.04 billion. Before moving to our outlook, I would like to provide a brief upgrade on expectations surrounding Foot Locker. First, as part of our cleanout of the garage action and broader merger and integration work, we continue to expect total pretax charges of up to $750 million. To date, we have recognized $520 million of these charges. The remaining pretax charges will be incurred through 2026 and over the medium term as we complete this work.

Sources indicate that specifically, for 2026, we continue to expect approximately $200 million from these acquisition-related charges, which have been excluded from today's non-GAAP EPS outlook. Second, we remain confident in achieving our previously announced $100 million to $125 million of cost synergies over the medium term, primarily from procurement and direct sourcing efficiencies. A portion of these synergy benefits are expected in 2026 and are reflected in our outlook. Now moving to our outlook for 2026. Our updated guidance reflects the continued strength of the DICK'S business and the progress we are making at Foot Locker, all within the context of dynamic geopolitical and macroeconomic environment.

In a recent development, within athletic footwear specifically, the marketplace remains promotional as the industry continues to work through elevated levels of legacy product. Against that backdrop, we are raising our full year expectation for DICK'S business, while maintaining our outlook for the Foot Locker business. Beginning with the DICK'S business, we now expect full year comp sales growth in the range of 3.3% to 4% compared to our prior comp growth expectation of 2.5% to 4%. We now expect full year operating income for DICK'S business in the range of $1.56 billion to $1.61 billion compared to our prior expectation of $1.54 billion to $1.6 billion. Turning to the Foot Locker business.

In a recent development, we continue to expect full year pro forma comp sales in the range of negative 2% to flat. We continue to expect full year operating loss for the Foot Locker business in the range of $80 million to $40 million. At the consolidated company level, we now expect full year non-GAAP earnings per diluted share in the range of $11.45 to $12.30 compared to our prior expectation of $11 to $12. Our earnings guidance is based on approximately 87.5 million average diluted shares outstanding compared to our prior expectation of approximately 90 million average diluted shares outstanding. We continue to anticipate a consolidated effective income tax rate of approximately 29% for the full year.

Industry observers note that for Q4, our earnings guidance assumes approximately 83 million average diluted shares outstanding and a net interest expense of approximately $30 million. Finally, from a capital allocation standpoint, we continue to invest in the business to strengthen our leadership position, drive profitable organic growth across the DICK'S business and support the turnaround at Foot Locker. And we now expect full year net capital expenditures of approximately $1.3 billion compared to our prior expectation of approximately $1.4 billion. The reduction reflects efficiencies we have identified across our capital program, while preserving the investment we believe are the most vital to our long-term growth.

According to recent reports, in closing, we are pleased with the continued strength of the DICK'S business and encouraged by the progress we are making at Foot Locker. Our updated outlook reflects confidence in the opportunities ahead, while maintaining appropriate measured view of the work still underway. We remain focused on strong execution as we close out the year. This concludes our prepared remarks. Thank you for your interest in DICK'S Sporting Goods. Operator, you may now open the line for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question comes from the line of Simeon Gutman from Morgan Stanley.

Simeon Gutman: I'd like to start with the DICK'S business maybe to Lauren. So you delivered another positive comp in Q3, and you mentioned a strong back-to-school season and market share gains. At the same time, the comp moderated a bit from Q2. So if you can walk us, please, through the puts and the takes behind the quarter.

Lauren R. Hobart: Yes. Thanks, Simeon. We were really pleased with the 2.6% comp we had in Q3 on top of a 5.7% comp, and we continue to gain market share. The quarter had a lot of significant wins in it. And I would point to the back-to-school season where we really did deliver broad-based growth with footwear outpacing the overall comp. That actually was the case for the entire quarter, really strong footwear growth, but also strong performance in team sports and license and trading cards and apparel through the back-to-school season. Our consumer is remaining really strong. And so as we've talked about for many quarters now, we are seeing growth in our overall database.

Industry observers note that we're actually having increased ScoreCard penetration and our athlete database is getting younger each year, which is just, I think, a testimony to the fact that we're bringing in so much newness and excitement. This quarter, we did also see all income demographics grow, and we didn't see trade down from best to better or better to good. So again, the consumer is going through a lot right now, but they are still prioritizing health and wellness, and they're certainly gravitating toward performance and newness and authenticity, and that's true across the entire portfolio. In October, as we all know, it was a very unseasonably warm October.

Industry observers note that and for us at DICK'S that's a time when the cold weather apparel categories are very heavy in our mix. So fleece is a big driver in October. That warm weather certainly affected our comps for the quarter and our transactions for the quarter. But the base business is doing really, really well. And as we look to the holiday, we're very excited about the areas of newness and giftable items throughout the entire assortment. So we feel really, really terrific about the business.

Recent findings suggest that simeon Gutman: Okay. The second part, maybe just for Ed. So last quarter, we spoke about a pretty tough athletic footwear and apparel marketplace, especially around the legacy footwear silhouettes. Can you talk about what has -- how the conditions evolved since then? How are you thinking about the duration of the promotional pressure? And looking further ahead, how should we think about Nike's planned Jordan reset and the potential impact on DICK'S and Foot Locker?

Sources indicate that edward W. Stack: Thanks, Simeon. We indicated that our footwear business last year was -- or last quarter was very good, but just under margin pressure due to too much inventory in the marketplace. And we feel that's still the same way. It's been primarily caused, as we've talked about, by too many legacy franchises and silhouettes, and that hasn't changed. Our team has really done a great job bringing new styles and new materials and embellishments into some of the legacy models, which have now started to do relatively well with those new materials and embellishments.

According to recent reports, we brought in new styles and broadened out some brands that are really doing extremely well in the marketplace, whether it's On, HOKA, Birkenstock, UGG and brands like that. So our footwear business, as we said, comped better than the company as a whole. So it's going to continue to be promotional through the balance of the quarter and maybe into -- a little bit into next year as we -- as everybody kind of cleans through that inventory. As far as the Jordan piece goes, I think it should be known that the Nike business at Foot Locker is really doing quite well. It's the Jordan business that's been difficult.

The decision Nike has made is, although a bit painful right now, is really the right decision for the Jordan brand for Nike and for Nike's partners. It's going to be really good for us going forward, but we're going to experience a little bit of pain here in the short term as they reset this business. So we're going to be a significant beneficiary of the Jordan change longer term, but it is going to be a little bit painful and more so for Foot Locker than for DICK'S going forward into next year.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Kate McShane from Goldman Sachs.

Katharine (Kate) McShane: It does seem like with regards to margins, you came in a little bit better than originally guided. So could you maybe walk through the dynamics of that? Did you not have to promote necessarily as much as you thought? Are you getting more vendor support than maybe you originally guided for? And how should we think about that dynamic through the end of the year?

In a recent development, edward W. Stack: I think there's a number of different things that we did. So was there some vendor support that we worked through? Yes. Did we have to promote quite as much? The silhouettes that needed to be promoted, that didn't change. But the team did a great job working the mix of bringing in some of these more in-demand products. The brands were helpful supporting us to get us that product. So we worked the mix a little bit there also. So it was -- it wasn't any one thing. It was a number of small things that our team really did a terrific job working through to help that margin rate.

Katharine (Kate) McShane: And then a follow-up question is, could you maybe patch us on how you're thinking about any kind of underperforming assets within the Foot Locker portfolio? Are there stores that are under active consideration for closures either in Europe or at other branches? And how should we think about the possibility of change there?

Edward W. Stack: Yes, there are -- we are definitely looking at stores that, as I noted in the script, are not meeting our profitability expectations. And there will be some stores that will close, and we're looking at those stores, and there'll be some across the globe, as you would imagine. There's stores in North America, in Europe, in Australia and New Zealand that aren't meeting our profitability expectations. And we don't see a path by which we could get them there. So they'll be closed, and we're starting to have these conversations with landlords about how we're going to go about that.

Recent findings suggest that we want to try to be fair to our landlords, but we also need to make sure that we do what's right for our business. So we're in active discussions today.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Brian Nagel from Oppenheimer.

In a recent development, brian Nagel: So first question I want to ask, this may be more for Ed, but on the more qualitative side, if you take the tone of the commentary today versus what we heard 3 months ago when you reported Q2 and some of the numbers, it seems like there's more confidence, right? So the question I want to ask is, I mean, a, am I hearing that correctly? But then maybe more importantly, if that's the case, is it more is DICK'S managing better than expected, a still tough environment? Or did the environment actually get better for DICK'S?

Industry observers note that edward W. Stack: Brian, I'd like to -- I don't know exactly how to say this, but I'm going to just try to say it. We didn't -- we never lost confidence. I think the Street kind of overreacted for whatever reason, and we understand that happens at times. But we were confident last time, we weren't happy about some of the promotional -- the promotional environment that we had to participate in. But as I noted in the last call, we really felt that participating in that promotional environment was really a great investment and the right investment to make in our business, but we had never really lost confidence. So we're extremely confident in our business.

It has been revealed that and I think you know us, we're somewhat conservative. There's got to be a lot of confidence for us to go out and buy 6.7 million shares of stock. And for the year, we're now up over 7 million shares of stock that we've repurchased. I think there's going to be a bumpy road with Foot Locker. It's going to be a bit bumpier than we had originally thought with what's going on with Jordan isn't helpful.

It has been revealed that A couple of other brands have been a little bit more difficult, but there's brands that's really working, and we're in the process of working through those brands, bringing in more of the product that maybe Foot Locker hadn't had before from an On standpoint, HOKA standpoint, and adding those brands into Foot Locker and into different banners inside Foot Locker. So we remain very confident. It's just going to be a little bit bumpier road. As far as DICK'S goes, we're extremely confident about the DICK'S business with what we're doing with House of Sport, Field House, what's going on with GameChanger.

Sources indicate that and I've often said GameChanger is our secret weapon of the data that we have with the youth sports and youth families. As we push into basketball with GameChanger, we couldn't be more excited about GameChanger. So on the DICK'S side, we're extremely confident, always have been. The Foot Locker side, we can kind of manage Foot Locker, and we've still got some work to do. We've got to work through some of the brands, and we've got to work through the Jordan issue. But we will work through that. And Nike is absolutely making the right decision of what they're doing with Jordan for the long term.

Sources indicate that and I applaud them for having the courage to make that long-term decision and look at the business over the long term as opposed to trying to -- for a quarter or 2. They're making the right -- we couldn't be happier with what they're doing.

According to recent reports, brian Nagel: That's very helpful. And my follow-up question is on Foot Locker. We talked before about the remodeling, the Fast Break locations. Maybe I missed it, but any revision there either how far you push into that remodeling of the performance of those units?

Edward W. Stack: When you say how far we push it, what do you mean? Are we going to do more of them or...

Brian Nagel: Like how many. Sorry, how many stores have now been remodeled?

Sources indicate that edward W. Stack: There's been -- we're up about 370 of them across the globe. I'd say we'll get close to 400 in the not-too-distant future.

Brian Nagel: And how are they performing now?

Industry observers note that edward W. Stack: They're outperforming the balance of the chain. We're pretty enthusiastic about it, especially as we reassort these stores with different product.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Christopher Horvers from JPMorgan.

Christopher Horvers: I want to dig into Foot Locker a little bit and then think about the Jordan reset for next year as well. So can you help us think about the drivers of that 4% U.S. comp? I guess how much was that -- would you attribute to the success of some of the Jordan introduces and the Caitlin versus unit performance and AUR recovery? And then more broadly, how significant is the potential headwind from the model count reduction in terms of Foot Locker's mix? I think there's -- as you look back over the past 6 years, Foot Locker merchandise margin is down like 600 basis points, clearly, probably selling some units, but at a very heavy discount.

So just want to think about the math of more full price selling versus the potential unit headwind that Jordan might create given the SKU count reduction?

Recent findings suggest that edward W. Stack: Well, I think of the 4% comp in North America, we're not going to -- the Jordan piece was an crucial part of that. As we talked about in our call last quarter, we said that we felt that the introduces in Q3 were going to be better than the launches in Q2. So that happened. Caitlin was important. Caitlin was probably more important for DICK'S than it was for Foot Locker, to be honest with you. And as we take a look at the headwinds with Jordan, we're still working through all of this with Nike. And Nike understands this. We're working through where we can get offsets in other styles and categories of product.

And our team is also working with other brands to take a look at how that we can offset what's going to happen from a Jordan standpoint. But we'll figure that. That's our job is to go figure these things out. And we're working through how to offset as much of the Jordan drop as we possibly can.

Christopher Horvers: I guess as you look back at Foot Locker's business prior to the acquisition, I mean, do you have a sense of what, I don't know, percentage full price selling or how much the AUR came off full price to try to drive some of those units and how just better in-stocks in key sizes and styles and high heat product can create an AUR tailwind that can provide a strong offset to what could be some unit headwinds?

According to recent reports, edward W. Stack: We think -- so I think you're looking at it the right way that there's going to be better in-stocks. There's going to be some -- we think more full price selling. You have to remember what happened with Foot Locker with Nike's modification to their go-to-market strategy when they went primarily DTC, a massive part of that was taking product away from Foot Locker. And they were taking product away from Foot Locker that was the high heat product. They were taking product away from Foot Locker that was -- that the retro side of the business didn't get access to some other parts of the Nike business.

And that was because they really didn't feel Foot Locker had invested in their business. They have not invested from a marketing standpoint. They were -- as Nike noted, they were an undifferentiated retailer. We're in the process of changing all of that. We've got Nike's full support along with the full support of other brands as we're doing this, and it's just going to take a little bit of time. But I would expect that there will be -- we are seeing more full price selling, and we will continue to see more full price selling going forward. And some of the AURs are picking up.

I mean, -- so I think you're looking at it the right way, and it's just going to take a little bit of time to do that.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your next question comes from the line of Adrienne Yih from Barclays.

It has been revealed that adrienne Yih-Tennant: Ed and Lauren, this is a bit of a higher-level question in terms of, can you help us -- there haven't been that many sort of marketplace inventory situations like this that most of us have gone through. So at the higher level, kind of based on your history, how does the process move from here? We're clearing through the inventory. There's probably -- holiday is a lot of volume, so we can get through a lot of it. Maybe a little hangover into the first half of next year. We've been through a number of Analyst Days, Investor Days across the vendors, tons of newness is coming to the marketplace, particularly back half of next year.

It has been revealed that so how does the infill restocking process work? Do we need to wait until fall season next year to see the demand reads? And are we looking at really '28 in terms of kind of getting a very good read on the newness flowing through? I mean in essence, how -- when and how swiftly can the rebalance of newness offset kind of some of the legacy?

Sources indicate that edward W. Stack: I think there's -- as we talked about, more inventory in the marketplace than we'd like. Foot Locker has a little bit more inventory than we would like also. Where the overage in Foot Locker's inventory is, it is in those legacy silhouettes. Some of those legacy silhouettes in basic colors are going to continue to sell. They're going to just sell at a lower rate -- a slower rate than in the past. And what our team is doing is filling in around those sizes and we're bringing in upcoming products. So that's kind of what's happened from an inventory standpoint.

Industry observers note that we will clear through that inventory and it will take through '27 because we don't want to just dump that inventory in the marketplace. There's no reason to do that. As we take a look at what's going on from a restocking standpoint, there's some newness coming into the marketplace. Caitlin is going to be terrific. We think what's going on with the Nike Mind shoe is great. We had a launch on that yesterday. It was terrific. So I don't think it's -- I don't think we have to wait as long as you're saying, but we're not really ready to go talk about '27 as of right now.

But we'll give you a very clear view on '27 at the end of our fourth quarter call.

Industry observers note that adrienne Yih-Tennant: Great. And then Navdeep, maybe without giving any guidance for '27, can you maybe talk to us about things we should consider, freight, oil, et cetera, as we kind of like turn the corner and our modeling into the first half? Again, no guidance, but just things that we should have top of mind in the model.

Edward W. Stack: Adrienne, before Navdeep answers that, I apologize. I just got called on to a vendor call that we've been trying to get taken care of. So I apologize, I've got to jump off, but Navdeep and Lauren can take it from here. I wish everybody a great Thanksgiving.

Sources indicate that navdeep Gupta: Actually, we'll share -- I would say some of the factors that you mentioned, the freight, the fuel as well as looking at some of the newness that you talked about are all the factors that we are considering in addition to what Ed mentioned around the Jordan allocation changes. On the DICK'S side, we continue to be extremely confident about the House of Sport and the Field House and the GameChanger growth opportunity. So as you think about the drivers on DICK'S, we continue to be excited about that we'll finish this year with 49 House of Sport store locations with well over 50 Field House locations and the GameChanger growth would be the drivers.

In a recent development, and on the economic side, like you called out, freight, fuel, we are also looking at other inflationary pressures that are within, and those would be the puts and takes. And we'll share much more of this at the next earnings call when we give our guidance for '27.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Michael Lasser from UBS.

According to recent reports, michael Lasser: It seems like given the performance in the third quarter, coupled with some of the commentary about the next few quarters, it's best for us to expect that the DICK'S banner will remain in this range, 2% to 3% from a comp perspective. Given that, is there enough flexibility in the cost structure to now reset to be able to generate expense leverage over the next few quarters, if indeed that is the right cadence for the business? And if not, are there enough gross margin good guys such that you can still experience some operating margin stability to expansion for that banner moving forward?

Sources indicate that lauren R. Hobart: Yes. Michael, I'll start, and I'll hand it to Navdeep. You're correct that our confidence in the DICK'S business remains strong and the balance of the portfolio, the broad base of the nature of the portfolio gives us a lot of confidence going forward. We absolutely have flexibility in our cost structure, and we are constantly focusing on how to drive expenses that will drive long-term capital improvements, long-term performance improvements. But Navdeep, I'll leave it to you to talk more about the flexibility.

Navdeep Gupta: Yes. Michael, I would build on what Lauren noted. As you can imagine, we have talked about these gross margin growth drivers with DICK'S Media Network and GameChanger. Those are continuing to be very differentiated drivers of not only our profitability, but our gross margin expansion. In addition to that, the work that our merchants keep doing in getting access to very differentiated product that is yielding really strong resonance with our athletes will be the driver. And on the SG&A side, I'm not ready to provide guidance as yet, but you can expect that the growth in our SG&A in 2027 will moderate from the growth that we are seeing in '26.

Michael Lasser: Got it. And my follow-up question is on the weather situation. Can you quantify how much you think the warm weather subtracted from the comp in the core DICK'S business in 3Q? What have you factored in for a similar type of condition in 4Q? And if it remains warm as we move through the rest of the holiday season, to what extent would that create some downward pressure on the profitability for this business as you have to clear out excess inventory? And to what degree has that been factored into your guidance for the core DICK'S banner for the fourth quarter?

Lauren R. Hobart: Great. Thanks, Michael. So looking back at Q3, we won't decomp it. But as I did mention, we had a very strong performance leading for the first 2 months of the quarter. So the weather certainly did impact us in the month of October. It is cold weather focused time frame. It is all about fleece and outerwear, and that business just didn't happen at that moment because of the extremely warm weather. But as we look to Q4, as you know, holiday time frame, we compete with so many different categories. We've got such a broad base of assortment. So certainly, it will get cold.

In a recent development, we will all be cold at some point during the holiday, but we are so much broader than that as we go into Black Friday and beyond. And I would just point to the fact that throughout our store right now, and I would encourage you to go in or look at the website, we have so many gifts for every single type of athlete, be it a trend-forward athlete who's looking at the footwear and apparel or kids who are looking at trading cards and collectibles and licensed and things for the performance athlete, be it the runner or the golfer, we have something for absolutely everybody. And so we are pumped. We are leaned into holiday.

I can't describe the energy that we have across our portfolio. Our store teams are pumped. And we will have a fantastic gift assortment for athletes this holiday.

Industry observers note that operator: Your next question comes from the line of Michael Baker from D.A. Davidson.

Sources indicate that michael Baker: Okay. Great. A couple on Foot Locker. It's kind of an ask, but maybe I'll ask it a different way. Just simply put, like the clearance in Foot Locker, where are you -- if you could maybe tell us an inning, where are you in this clearance process that really started last quarter or at the very least, is it going faster than you expected, slower than expected? Just some way to sort of give us some sense as to where you are in that process? And where is the light at the end of the tunnel?

According to recent reports, lauren R. Hobart: Yes. Michael, obviously, this is not just a DICK'S matter. This is an industry category issue. There's just a lot of product in the marketplace. But the best proof point I can give you is that last quarter, it was a very material part of our margin, especially at Foot Locker, our sales and our margin. And this quarter, at least in the North America business, the Foot Locker team was able to put up a 4% comp. So those pressures existed throughout the quarter, and they were still able to do that. So I would say this is going to be a long process.

Recent findings suggest that just as Ed said, it's not going to happen overnight, but we will buy around it. We will bring in other things that are new, and we will get through it. I'm very pleased with how the team navigated it last quarter.

Michael Baker: Yes. That sounds reasonable. And actually, my follow-up question was going to be exactly on that point. U.S. up 4%. I think North America up, I think you said 1% and change. Total Foot Locker up 0.5%. I guess what's different about the U.S.? Is it just timing that you've gotten to it? Or is there something different? I guess the point of the question is, can we expect 4% for Foot Locker? Is that what's coming as you do these changes? Or is the U.S. for some reason, just going to be better than the other parts of the portfolio?

Lauren R. Hobart: Yes. Great question. The U.S. is certainly, a, where we have focused the first part of our efforts. So the increased assortment, Fast Break stores all started in the U.S. That was where we were able to dive in the moment we acquired the organization. But in general, we've been pretty clear that EMEA is a bigger challenge than the U.S. is. And that has to do with the industry there. It has to do with consumer pressure. The geopolitical environment is harsher in EMEA and so the macroeconomic impacts there as well.

According to recent reports, so EMEA is going to be a longer slog than North America, and we are continuing to take the lessons of things that are working here and translate them. They have launched Fast Break now. They launched a marketing campaign, and we are continuing to work on both sides of the business. I do think North America has got a head start against EMEA.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Bob Drbul from BTIG.

Robert (Bob) Drbul: I just have 2 quick questions, if I could. The first one is on the GameChanger business. Can you just talk a bit more around what you're seeing, I think, with the addition of basketball and the engagement that you're seeing throughout the DICK'S business generally? And then just a quick follow-up on the Foot Locker piece. I think Ed had mentioned that the Jordan piece was struggling, but the Nike business was doing better in Foot Locker. Could you possibly expand a bit on that commentary?

Lauren R. Hobart: Great. Okay, Bob. Thanks for the question on GameChanger because this is, as Ed mentioned, really the secret weapon in our arsenal. It is an incredibly exciting digital, one of the #1 youth sports apps in the country. And what's been amazing in 10 years to think back, and we've been really celebrating the 10-year anniversary this November, but to think back that the company had $8 million in revenue and now $150 million last year and approaching $200 million. It's also extremely profitable. So you heard us talk earlier about gross margin and the fact that there were some offsets to some of the pressure we had with our merch margin.

Well, some of those offsets are things like the GameChanger business and the DICK'S Media Network, which are non-merchandise revenue that are resulting in margin gains, and GameChanger is a great contributor to that. With regard to diamond, diamond is where GameChanger has been born and grown up. It's a really terrific share market in diamond sports. But we have our sights set on multiple different categories. And the next flag that we are planting is in basketball. We've got a terrific product that we just rolled out this past season. And in basketball, there's 13 million kids who play basketball.

So we're taking all of the amazing technology that we have built with AI and with all of the live streaming and scoring and stats that we have with diamond, and we're translating it to a basketball athlete, and we're very excited about that. The other thing I'm going to say about GameChanger is that it's a really important part of our DICK'S Media Network across the board. It's got live sports in a platform that really nobody else can reach athletes through a time when they are fully engaged and watching kids live. So really feel great about the Jordan business -- I'm sorry, GameChanger business. Your next question on Jordan.

We are seeing growth across several Nike businesses at Foot Locker and DICK'S. The Nike Mind shoe is doing very well. #85101. 19 Signs Your Company’s Technology Is Creating More Work

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1378 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

19 Signs Your Company’s Technology Is Creating More Work

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1378 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Technology should simplify workflows and improve productivity.
  • In a recent development, these workarounds can reveal deeper problems with technology adoption, system design and organizational processes.
  • According to recent reports, the biggest tell for me is hearing, “Here’s how we actually do it.” If that follows with some description that combines spreadsheets, duplicate data entry, manual handoffs or clever ways around the system, that’s a pretty clear sign the technology is creating work rather than removing it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Technology should simplify workflows and improve productivity. However, when systems are difficult to navigate, unreliable or disconnected, employees may develop alternative solutions just to get their jobs done.

In a recent development, these workarounds can reveal deeper problems with technology adoption, system design and organizational processes. Below, Forbes Technology Council members share warning signs that employees are spending too much time working around their company’s technology rather than benefiting from it, along with insights on addressing the underlying complications.

According to recent reports, the biggest tell for me is hearing, “Here’s how we actually do it.” If that follows with some description that combines spreadsheets, duplicate data entry, manual handoffs or clever ways around the system, that’s a pretty clear sign the technology is creating work rather than removing it. - Abhijit Singh, Jefferson.

If employees constantly ask coworkers for help with the same system tasks or there’s an unofficial cheat sheet, chat thread or go-to “expert” everyone relies on to navigate a tool, the technology is not intuitive enough to be used on its own. Low adoption of mandatory tools or latest hires taking too long to be productive with a tool are indicators that people are spending too much time figuring out the technology instead of using it. - Austin Berglas, Nardello & Co.

Sources indicate that forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

Working around a system can increase your cognitive load—the mental effort placed on your working memory. A recent survey found that since AI was introduced, enterprise workers spend longer searching for information, parse through more alerts, and juggle more tabs and applications. Symptoms like these can indicate employees are working harder to manage the technology than realizing its benefits. - Mazy Dar, HERE Enterprise (here.io).

Jumping across multiple tools and screens to complete one workflow is a clear sign that people are just becoming workers for the tools rather than using those tools to deliver their work better and faster. This is more relevant in the AI era. - Raja Shanmugam, TATA Consultancy Services.

Recent findings suggest that when employees rely on personal texts, phone calls or spreadsheets to compensate for enterprise systems, there’s a workflow problem. These workarounds often emerge because existing tools are too slow, fragmented or unreliable. Leaders should investigate where employees bypass technology and address the underlying friction before it creates operational risks. - Judit Sharon, OnPage Corporation.

Watch for employees delaying decisions because they don’t trust how current the information is. If a sales or marketing team has to wait for an overnight revision before responding to a customer or adjusting a campaign, the technology is setting the pace instead of supporting the work. Teams should be able to act on what is happening now, not yesterday’s picture. - Vibhor Kapoor, AdRoll.

Industry observers note that one sign is that unofficial spreadsheets become essential to completing everyday work. In capital markets, employees may repeatedly export trade data, reconcile it manually, and re-enter the results across systems. When these workarounds become routine, the technology is shifting effort onto employees rather than removing it. Those spreadsheets reveal where workflows need fixing. - Lakshmanan Alagappan, Genpact UK.

Sources indicate that shadow documentation is a sign that the official documentation is lacking or so generic that it is hard to adapt to use cases that are fairly common. The more guides that are built to explain how to use a piece of software, the more it should be evaluated for improvement. Simplify the interface with role-based views, and rename custom fields and data so they’re clearer. Just don’t forget to clean up the shadow documentation too. - Luke Wallace, Bottle Rocket.

One sign is that the know-how lives in people, not the system. When a tool doesn’t do exactly what’s needed, rather than asking for changes to the tool, work becomes manual, and one person ends up as the only one who knows how it really runs. Sometimes that’s accidental and sometimes it’s job security; either way, it’s a bottleneck. - Anila Siraj, OpsBridge Advisory.

One sign is employees building integrations the vendor never intended. Not plugins. Not configurations. Custom code written at midnight by someone who needed two systems to talk to each other and could not wait six months for a roadmap update. That unauthorized integration is not ingenuity. It is your architecture silently fracturing one undocumented API call at a time. When engineers route around the system, the system has already failed. - Mukul Arora.

People clicking straight through warnings is a sign. Track override rates and fix the friction behind them. If employees routinely hit “proceed anyway” on a blocked link or a security prompt, the tool is getting in the way of real work, and they have stopped reading it. That is a workaround too, albeit a quiet one, and it trains them to ignore warnings—maybe even those that matter. - Flavius Plesu, OutThink.

In a recent development, one clear sign is when employees spend more time figuring out how to make a tool work than doing their actual jobs. If everyone knows which buttons to avoid, which errors to ignore and when to restart the system, your technology isn’t saving time. It’s wasting it. - Margarita Simonova, ILoveMyQA.

According to recent reports, check the expense reports, not the help desk tickets. When employees start reimbursing themselves for $30 SaaS subscriptions, they’ve already given up on the official tools and bought their way around them. Finance sees it first. IT sees it months later. The line items are small enough to approve without question, which is exactly why they keep adding up. - Nidhi Jain, CloudEagle.ai.

In a recent development, map the value stream from user intent to task outcome. If employees are required to navigate more than three non-value-added steps to complete a task, I’d question the process before adding more steps. Workarounds add effort yet little to no customer value. Even worse is when teams automate workarounds when they should be eliminating the reason it exists in the first place. - April Ho-Nishimura, Infineon Technologies AG.

When I ask a client team how their leadership report is produced, a common answer is that someone builds a spreadsheet by hand before every meeting. That tells me the official systems are being worked around. The hours are the visible cost. The bigger one is that leaders start questioning the numbers in the room instead of making decisions. - Dimitar Dimitrov, Accedia.

Count the decisions the technology changed last week. Many companies hand managers a data platform and announce that every number is in there, ready for any table they want. Almost nobody opens it because it asks them to become analysts. They keep deciding using their gut and old reports. A tool that shows each manager their own score and the next move gets checked daily. If a system doesn’t trigger decisions, it is overhead. - Vivek Thomas, AISensum.

According to recent reports, you must watch how often employees double-check a tool’s output before acting on it. If a manager has to pull the original records to verify every report, the system may be saving time on preparation while adding it back in review. So, ask what people still check by hand and why. That extra checking is part of the cost of the tool, too. - Elton Chan, Second Talent.

It has been revealed that take a construction site where the real system is WhatsApp. A delivery gets redirected to another site in a group chat; nobody updates the records, materials arrive at the wrong site, and machinery stands idle. When orders change in chats and handwritten logs, the ERP is just a reporting duty. Count how many changes never reach your system of record. - Andrew Babkin, Azati.

In a recent development, one sign is when employees lower the quality of their work because company technology cannot support enough detail. Engineers may simplify technical assessments, while customer service teams may give incomplete responses because systems restrict what they can record or process. Leaders should check whether technology limitations influence the quality of business outcomes. Technology should support professional judgment, not force employees to compromise it. - Salice Thomas, Wipro Limited.

The company raised its full-year 2026 guidance for sales and earnings, reflecting progress in its proprietary brand portfolio and marketplace expansion. To prepare for the holiday season, the company is scaling its gifting assortment and expanding same-day delivery through partnerships with DoorDash, Uber Eats, and Instacart.

It has been revealed that michael J. Bender: Thank you, Trevor. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today for Kohl's third quarter 2026 earnings conference call. Before I begin today, I want to take a moment to thank our entire team at Kohl's. Each day is an opportunity to serve our customers, and the initiatives we've outlined are focused on improving our customers' experience. We've made great progress thus far, but additional key work remains ahead. Thank you for your dedication and commitment to Kohl's. I would also like to extend a warm welcome to Ryan Waymire, who joined Kohl's as Chief Merchandising Officer at the end of September.

It has been revealed that since arriving, Ryan has hit the ground running, visiting stores, collaborating with his merchandising teams, connecting with vendors and brand partners, and hearing directly from our customers. We're thrilled to leverage his deep expertise and leadership as part of our executive team. Our performance in the third quarter reflects the tangible progress we are making against our strategic initiatives, highlighted by a return to top-line growth with 1.2% positive comparable sales. As we make steady progress on our strategic initiatives, our customers are responding favorably, driving broad-based improvements across the business. While this is an encouraging milestone, we know crucial work remains ahead.

In a recent development, additionally, our focus on operating the business with discipline continues to pay off as we expanded our operating margin and increased earnings per share. We continue to solidify our balance sheet, and our cash generation remains strong. The progress and ongoing execution will continue to deliver a sustainable financial framework that allows us to invest in the business and return capital to shareholders through our dividend and share repurchase programs. I would also like to acknowledge that we are operating in a challenging macroeconomic environment. The core customers that we serve are facing inflationary pressures in their daily expenses that are altering their behaviors when shopping discretionary categories.

While customers have remained resilient, it is clear that they are migrating to value with their purchases. Our strategic initiatives directly address these customer priorities. As we head into the holiday, we remain dedicated to providing compelling value to our customers through our product offerings. Now let me share some additional highlights from our performance that give us confidence that we are moving in the right direction. First, every line of business delivered a positive comp. The work we focused on throughout the year to elevate product relevance for our customer is starting to pay off, with positive results across every major category: women's, men's, kids, footwear, home, and accessories.

Second, our priority brands continue to resonate with our customers and delivered a positive 3.4% comparable sales performance in the quarter. These brands play an important role in our brand portfolio and value proposition. Our By Kohl's brands provide quality products at compelling price points, which is especially important in the current economic backdrop we are operating in. Third, over the past year, we have developed strategic targeted actions to re-engage our Kohl's Card customers. This important cohort represents our most productive and loyal customer base. We have made great progress listening to this customer and delivering products and experiences that they look for when shopping at Kohl's.

Recent findings suggest that this ongoing work resulted in an improved comparable sales performance to a +2.6% with our Kohl's Card customers in the quarter. Fourth, the investments we are making into our store experience are making a difference. We have made investments into brand amplification, reduced redundancy across the floor, and invested in inventory to deliver greater trip assurance and consistency across our store fleet. While early in this work, we saw our stores return to growth and deliver a 2% comparable sales increase in the third quarter. Next, let me provide details on our three key initiatives and the progress we are making to deliver a better customer experience.

It has been revealed that beginning with our first initiative, offering a curated and more balanced assortment that fulfills the needs of all customers. This initiative focuses on addressing customer demand by clarifying assortments, elevating product relevance, and offering the key items and categories shoppers want. While there is still more work ahead in this initiative, our work is resonating with customers in the third quarter. Every line of business improved sequentially versus prior quarter and delivered a positive comp. Starting with the women's business, we returned to growth in the third quarter with a 0.5% comparable sales increase. Strength continues to be led by our juniors business, which delivered its fourth straight quarter of high-single-digit comparable sales increases.

In addition, we revealed a strong performance in our denim business, with proprietary denim up over 30% and Levi's up high-single-digits. We saw outperformance in our transition to cool weather goods with fleece and long-sleeve tees up low teens, and we expect this momentum to continue in the fourth quarter. Our intimates and sleepwear businesses were pressured in the quarter, and we continue to make progress with our reduced choice counts and improved depth, which is especially crucial to these categories. Moving to our men's business, which delivered a +1.5% comparable sales performance. This 240 basis point improvement from Q2 was a result of the work we have been doing to deliver a more clear and simplified shopping experience.

We've made great progress in this category, editing out redundancies and investing into key programs that resonate with our customers. A great example of this is within our FLX brand, which continues to grow at an outstanding pace and has developed into a top brand in our men's department. Within active, we've also experienced strength from Tek Gear and Nike apparel. Our dress category also delivered strong performance in the quarter, up 11%, highlighted by Haggar. Softness in the men's business was driven by sportswear, which is still in the process of editing through assortments to provide improved clarity. Now let me move to our kids business, which accelerated to a +1.3% comp in the third quarter.

Kids continues to experience outsized performance within our toys business from trending products like LEGO, KPop Demon Hunters, and NeeDoh squishies. We're well-positioned to build on this momentum as we head into the holiday season, as toys and gifting becomes a higher penetration of our business. Within kids apparel, we're seeing solid results from our fall seasonal merchandise with key brands like FLX Kids and SO. Although early, we are pleased with the initial results we saw within our baby and infant category, where we recently reintroduced the offering of our opening price point proprietary brand, Jumping Beans. Additionally, our Babies“R”Us initiative delivered another quarter of positive growth.

In a recent development, this September, we completed 56 additional Babies“R”Us shop build-outs and recently rolled out accessories towers in nearly all stores offering our highest velocity gifts and accessories. As we anticipated, our footwear business returned to growth in the third quarter, generating a 4% positive comp. This marks over a 700 basis point improvement from just the second quarter. Highlights include improved newness and depth in key brands like Nike, adidas, and Skechers, all delivering positive comparable sales. Additionally, we're excited about the performance we saw within our boots business, which was heavily impacted by tariffs last fall. In the third quarter, boots grew over 20% versus prior year, and we expect positive momentum in boots to continue into the fourth quarter.

Our accessories business improved and delivered a +0.7% comparable sales performance. Excluding Sephora, our accessories business maintained its mid-single-digit growth trend, led by impulse, jewelry, and luggage. Impulse continued its strong momentum, delivering more than a 20% comparable sales increase. Through this initiative, we are able to offer frequent newness and great value to our customers, featuring everyday essentials and small gifting items. Jewelry continued its momentum, achieving its second straight quarter of mid-single-digit growth. In October, we expanded elevated fashion jewelry displays and fine jewelry case lines across more than 300 locations. Looking ahead, we see further opportunity to build the presence of this important gifting category across our omnichannel platforms.

According to recent reports, our Sephora at Kohl's business ran down 1.9% versus prior year. Although this continues to underperform the organization, the Q3 results mark a 200 basis point improvement from Q2. We experienced continued pressure in the third quarter from a few of our top brands as they recently expanded their distribution. To partially offset some of this pressure, we partnered closely with Sephora to curate an offering of differentiated products and experiences for our customers. This includes expanded gifting and value sets, new travel-sized assortments, exciting brand releases, and unlocking same-day delivery for Sephora customers by leveraging our DoorDash and Instacart partnerships.

It has been revealed that looking deeper, fragrance remained a bright spot in the third quarter with outperformance in key brands like YSL, KAYALI, and Valentino. Our makeup business improved from Q2 by nearly 400 basis points in the third quarter, led by the rollout of MAC to all stores, which continues to exceed our expectations. We saw additional strength from prestige brands such as Charlotte Tilbury and Merit. Skincare continues to be the biggest challenge as we lap expanded distribution headwinds. This fall, we have introduced a lot of newness in the skincare business with exciting brands like Beauty of Joseon in the K-beauty category and Salt & Stone in the body category, both of which are off to strong starts.

Sources indicate that home continued to improve their business in the third quarter, delivering a 1% comp increase. This performance was driven by strength in electronics and bath categories. In small electrics, we continue to see newness and innovation resonate with customers, with key national brands Shark, Ninja, and KitchenAid posting strong double-digit comparable sales increases. Within our seasonal décor business, we were able to right-size our depth and invest more into choice counts. We are pleased with the customer response in our harvest and holiday décor businesses. Next, let me move to our second initiative, re-establishing Kohl's as a leader in value and quality.

According to recent reports, in today's environment, it is evident that our customers have become increasingly choiceful with their discretionary spending as their budgets remain under pressure. Customers are looking to stretch every dollar, and we know how vital it is to meet their needs, especially this upcoming holiday season. Our goal is to firmly position Kohl's as a trusted destination where families can consistently find excellent quality and relevant styles at compelling price points. We are delivering value through several avenues in order to deepen customer engagement while also attracting upcoming shoppers. This work begins with elevating our proprietary brand portfolio, which, as I mentioned before, delivered over 3% sales growth in the third quarter.

Sources indicate that these brands match affordability with modern style and continue to play an essential role in our assortment. In Q3, we made further progress enhancing these brands by increasing inventory depth while also investing into the in-store experience and scaling our marketing efforts to effectively build awareness for new and existing customers. Brands like SO, FLX, and LC Lauren Conrad continue to lead our apparel assortment, while brands like Miryana and Mingle & Co. drove strong performances in home. Additionally, we continue to discover new ways to enhance our ability to connect with customers throughout their shopping journey.

In a recent development, this includes leveraging targeted offers to deepen our engagement with our savvy Kohl's Card customers, who love the additional discounts they receive as Kohl's most loyal shoppers. Lastly, we saw a strong response from customers during our Kohl's Deal Days event in early October. This event highlighted broader and more simplified value messaging across key brands and categories to showcase the value we are offering. We are building on this success to provide exceptional value throughout our shopping experience. Our gifting and impulse business continues to become more impactful and serves to drive incremental units in our customers' baskets.

Recent findings suggest that our toy towers and deal bars are driving momentum by providing a compelling assortment of toys and home décor at price points under $10. Finally, our back-to-school offerings included thousands of back-to-school items priced under $25 to fit all budgets, all of which delivered strong results in the third quarter. Turning to our third initiative, building a frictionless omnichannel experience. Our teams made measurable progress in the third quarter across our inventory, store experience, and digital capabilities. Starting with our inventory management and allocation, disciplined merchandise planning remains foundational to our operating model. By establishing more timely, targeted inventory flows, we drove stronger full-price sell-through across key seasonal categories, reflected in our fall seasonal business increasing low single digits.

It has been revealed that A core component of this inventory management and allocation is tailored to deliver trip assurance. We are intentionally simplifying the shopping experience by increasing our apparel inventory depth by mid-teens while trimming total choice counts by high teens. This deliberate shift delivers improved clarity and ensures our core high-demand items are reliably in stock. In addition, we are refining our allocation algorithms to better support lower-volume stores, ensuring a more consistent shopping experience across our store fleet. While still early in this work, we are already seeing the payoff as stores delivered positive comparable sales in the quarter. Another way to support our stores is through a more elevated experience.

Industry observers note that our store fleet serves as a competitive advantage for Kohl's, as we are investing in an enhanced in-store environment to drive engagement and conversion. This September, we rolled out this elevated experience to nearly all of our stores, highlighting our By Kohl's brands. These dedicated areas feature upgraded outfitting mannequins, clear navigation signage, and find your fit guides that make styling and self-service easier. Additionally, we are testing a strengthened brand and storytelling presentation with key brands like Nike and Levi's. Finally, on digital modernization, we are evolving our digital ecosystem to give customers inspiration and flexibility in how they shop. We continue to be encouraged by the initial results from our Ask Kohl's agentic shopping assistant.

In a recent development, customers who engaged with Ask Kohl's are finding a more personalized experience, driving higher conversion and revenue per visit. In today's retail environment, customers are prioritizing speed and convenience. To capitalize on this, we recently launched same-day delivery offerings through partnerships at DoorDash and Uber Eats to complement our Instacart partnership. We are pleased with the start of this strategy and believe there is further opportunity to leverage our large and conveniently located store base to reach our customers. Additionally, we launched Klarna earlier this month, which provides a flexible payment option for our customers. Now, I would like to provide a brief patch on how we are positioned for the key holiday season.

Sources indicate that our focus is on solidifying Kohl's as the go-to destination for value, gifting, and convenience. Consumers remaining highly choiceful with their spending, how we show up will be even more key. Knowing this, we identified three primary areas of focus this holiday. First, offering a sharpened value in our assortment. We are meeting budget-conscious shoppers with clear, compelling value, featuring $5-$20 opening price point gifts and impulse stocking stuffers. Freshness will be front and center, with nearly half of our holiday gift shop assortment being completely new this year, with the vast majority priced under $15. At the same time, we have scaled gifting across our destination categories.

This includes expanding our fine jewelry presence, dedicated in-store toy towers featuring items under $10, and curating over 2,000 Sephora prestige beauty gifts under $30. The Sephora partnership continues to be an incredible traffic driver, bolstered this season by exciting latest brand arrivals and gift sets. Second, an engaging marketing campaign. Our holiday campaign, The North Kohl's, bridges inspiring brand storytelling with purposeful basket building. In our stores, we have simplified the shopping journey by creating curated discovery hubs such as the Cozy Corner, Style Square, and Hosting Headquarters, designed to drive cross-category conversion.

Sources indicate that across all media channels, we are leaning into broader, simplified promotional messaging to ensure our value proposition cuts through the holiday noise, particularly during peak volume moments, including Black Friday, Cyber Week, and the post-Christmas clearance window. Third, enabling frictionless omnichannel execution. Winning the holiday season requires exceptional operational agility, and we are meeting our customers however they choose to shop by launching our new AI-powered digital shopping assistant, integrating flexible payment options at checkout, and significantly expanding same-day delivery. Furthermore, for shoppers prioritizing speed and convenience right down to the wire, most of our buy online, pick up in store orders will be fulfilled and ready within two hours straight through Christmas Eve.

According to recent reports, we are excited about the strategy we have underway, and we are ready to serve our customers this holiday season. With that, I would like to hand the call over to Jill.

Dycom (DY -18.02%) reported third quarter results that exceeded the high end of its guidance across all primary financial metrics, including revenue, adjusted EBITDA, and adjusted EPS. Management raised the tech giant's full-year revenue outlook to a range of $7.66 billion to $7.73 billion, supported by a record total backlog of $12.9 billion. 10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most anticipated initial public offerings (IPOs) in market history has finally gone public. Anthropic (ANT -6.54%), the company behind Claude, priced its offering at $83, above the initial target. Those shares began trading on Nov. 19, opening at $111.50 before finishing their debut session at $97.17, still 17% above the IPO price.

Dario Amodei. Image source: Getty Images.

It has been revealed that the company raised a whopping $81.3 billion, making it the largest public debut ever, surpassing even Space Exploration Technologies' (SPCX -5.65%) mega-IPO earlier this year. And at Thursday's close, Anthropic was worth $1.76 trillion on a fully diluted basis, instantly making it one of the largest public companies on the planet.

If you manage to get ahold of $5,000 in Anthropic stock, what might that investment look like five years from now?

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/24/26.

According to recent reports, anthropic brought in $41 million in revenue in 2023 and $4.6 billion in 2025, then did $33.2 billion in just the first nine months of 2026, up roughly 1,200% from the same stretch a year earlier. That is incredible growth that we really haven't seen at this scale.

The bull case centers around this continuing. The bet is that Claude gets embedded in business processes across industries, and the sort of wholesale transformation of work we've seen in coding happens elsewhere.

One of the most encouraging figures for the bull thesis is Anthropic's net revenue retention, which sits at about 900%. That means customers find Claude valuable enough not only to stick around, but to scale their usage -- and spending -- ninefold in a single year.

Industry observers note that the bear case is really centered around what all that growth costs. Anthropic's amended filing indicated about $895 billion in purchase commitments and leases, mostly for compute and infrastructure -- the chips and data centers its models run on. About half of that is due before the end of 2030. And while Anthropic notched an operating gain in Q2 this year, it swung back to a $567 million operating loss in Q3.

Industry observers note that and then, of course, the bear case also assumes the incredible revenue growth we've seen slows down considerably. In the bear case, Claude remains highly valuable in the programming world, but its broader use across most of the rest of the economy is limited.

Here are a few scenarios sketched out.

Industry observers note that the truth is that it is remarkably hard to predict where a stock like Anthropic's will be even a year from now. This truly is terra incognita.

That mentioned, I believe it will be closest to the bear case. I'm not sure investors appreciate just how precarious Anthropic's position is. It must commit to spending on compute and infrastructure well before it actually books the corresponding revenue. And with usage-based billing, its customers' spending habits can turn on a dime.

My biggest glitch is that I fail to see a durable moat. I think the most likely scenario is that artificial intelligence (AI) will look more like a commodity in a few years, and that Anthropic will find that its customers are happy to look elsewhere if it means they can pay less.

By Anders Bylund – Nov 24, 2026 at 4:26PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Analog Devices ›.

Industry observers note that analog Devices (ADI -17.37%) reported fourth-quarter results early Tuesday morning. The analog and mixed-signal chip designer crushed Wall Street's consensus estimates and followed up with in-line guidance.

Recent findings suggest that and investors hated it. The stock fell as much as 19.7% in the morning session, recovering slightly to a 16.6% drop as of 3:23 p.m. ET.

Analog Devices' headline figures were great in Q4 2026. Earnings rose 80% year-over-year to $4.06 per share. Revenues jumped 42% to $4.37 billion. The analyst consensus had called for earnings near $3.89 per share on roughly $4.32 billion in top-line sales. The guidance ranges for next quarter were broadly in line with current Street projections.

But the drop makes sense when you dig below the usual numbers. Q1 revenue guidance is in line with Street expectations, but it's still a disappointing slowdown after a fantastic Q4 result. Operating margins will fall due to high component costs and holiday-season factory shutdowns.

Moreover, Analog Devices' chip-making facilities are running at full capacity, limiting the manufacturer's ability to actually take on more orders. More manufacturing capacity is on the way with a 150% year-over-year increase in capital expenditures, but the new production lines won't make any chips until the second half of 2028.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/24/26.

Industry observers note that analog Devices is a victim of its own roaring success. When your factories are already humming at full tilt and channel inventories are finally back to normal levels, there simply isn't much room left for upside surprises in the near term.

Instead of another beat-and-raise quarter, shareholders are getting a massive $1.6 billion to $1.9 billion capital spending bill next year -- and they won't see a single chip roll off those new lines until fiscal year 2028. The stock entered this report priced for perfection, trading at a beefy 37 times trailing earnings after Tuesday's massive drop. From there, in-line guidance and a long wait for the next growth spurt were all the excuse traders needed to hit the eject button.

Erling Haaland has unveiled a dramatic new look after cutting off his trademark blond locks.

The Manchester City striker revealed his new buzzcut hairstyle on Sunday morning ahead of his side’s Premier League opener at home to Bournemouth later in the day.

Later in the episode, Haaland called a host of famous faces, including Oasis singer Noel Gallagher and former City manager Pep Guardiola, to get their opinions on his transformation.

Recent findings suggest that pep Guardiola's reaction to Erling Haaland's latest haircut. 😭😂📲 Watch: https://t.co/4KvxC9e5mx pic.twitter.com/QQBCKKpGkP.

Haaland, 26, has not sported short hair since his time at Borussia Dortmund, where he played three seasons before joining City in 2022.

Haaland removed his hairband during a 4-1 win over Arsenal in 2023 on a raucous night at the Etihad as City beat their title rivals to move one step closer to winning the league. There will be no need for one now, though, with a close-cut look to mark a new campaign.

It is a new-look City in more ways than one this term with head coach Enzo Maresca looking to kickstart a new era following Pep Guardiola’s exit.

Maresca is hoping for an immediate return to form in City’s Premier League opener after a chastening 3-0 defeat by Arsenal in the Community Shield last week.

So far, only Elliot Anderson has arrived but Maresca is hopeful the club will be active in the transfer market. Rodri has left for Barcelona while Savinho is closing in on a move to Tottenham.

In a recent development, “I’ll try to find a new Rodri – it is what it is,” the former Chelsea manager stated. “Rodri, before he arrived here, he didn’t win the Ballon d’Or, he didn’t win the Champions League, he didn’t win the Club World Cup. Then he joined the club and then after he achieved many key things. Now the target for us is to try to find the new Rodri.

Industry observers note that “When David Silva was here, everyone was worried - Kevin [De Bruyne] arrived. When Sergio Agüero was here, everyone was worried – Erling [Haaland] arrived. When Ferdinando left, Rodri arrived. It’s just about this.

“When they leave, you need to be good and recruit the next one. They are all similar – David, Kevin, Fernandinho, Rodri, Agüero, Erling. It’s just normal, it’s a change. It’s not a problem, just go again and try to do the right things.”.

Recent findings suggest that maresca added: “Hopefully we can do the things that we need to do. It doesn’t help that there are players that for different reasons want to leave, this is for sure.

“But we need to adapt and we don’t want to keep players here that don’t want to stay.

“The normal thing in transfer windows is that you have to wait because all the clubs try to keep players until the last week and then sell for more money.

Industry observers note that “It’s normal, I’m not worried about that. When the transfer window closes and we have all the squad there, for sure it will be different.”.
